problem_shape: These papers are about making digital shape behave like a trustworthy object instead of a loose collection of samples. A mesh, meaning a surface stored as many small connected triangles or quads, may need to be measured, cleaned, simplified, animated, printed, textured, cut into panels, or compared with another surface. The shared difficulty is that the visible object is continuous, but the computer often holds it as pieces: vertices, faces, rays, fields, slices, correspondences, tokens, or captured points. If the pieces are changed independently, the object can tear, cross itself, lose sharp edges, blur texture, break inside-out tests, or become too slow to query. The family therefore keeps asking the same question in different forms: what relationships must remain true while the representation changes? Some papers preserve appearance while remaking triangles, some preserve distance or winding tests while accelerating queries, some preserve cloth, garment, skeleton, or toolpath structure while adapting shape to motion or manufacture. The common object is not just a shape, but a shape plus the rules that make it usable.
naive_failure: A smart beginner might try to treat every small piece of geometry separately. To compare two surfaces, check every triangle against every other triangle. To clean a tangled surface, push intersecting faces apart locally. To preserve a texture, keep the old image and hope the new triangles still line up. To generate an artist-style surface, list faces one by one. To print a non-planar object, slice it into simple layers and connect nearby paths. These attempts fail because shape errors are relational. A small local fix can create a global wrongness: an inside becomes outside, a sharp feature rounds off, a garment no longer matches a body, a cloth frame no longer agrees with nearby frames, or a toolpath collides after a layer looks valid by itself. Brute force also fails at scale. Exact distance, winding, intersection, and surface evaluation become expensive when every query must inspect too many pieces.
mathematical_principle: The recurring principle is to turn shape into constraints that can be measured and preserved while the representation changes. Distance methods measure the worst mismatch between two surfaces, then avoid useless work by proving that whole regions cannot contain the answer. Winding-number methods measure whether a point is inside by adding the signed influence of the surrounding surface, then reduce that addition to faster ray or boundary calculations. Remeshing and offsetting preserve visible appearance, sharp features, and correspondence, meaning the new pieces must still point back to the same parts of the old object. Untangling and panelization adjust vertices or surface flows while penalizing intersections, stress, or loss of fidelity. Generation and capture papers use fields, correspondences, and aggregations to carry hidden structure such as skeletons, skin weights, garment-body matches, wrinkle motion, or surface signals. The math matters because it defines what counts as wrong: too far away, crossing when it should not, losing an edge, changing density, breaking endpoint distributions, or violating toolpath thickness. Once wrongness is measurable, algorithms can search, subdivide, simplify, or stop early with a reason.
why_math_matters: The mathematics is not decoration because surfaces contain structure that the eye, the printer, the simulator, and downstream tools all depend on. A triangle list alone does not say which side is inside, which edge is intentionally sharp, which texture sample belongs to which point, or whether two nearby folds are allowed to touch. Boundary integrals, ray tests, Hausdorff bounds, convex hulls, and Lipschitz limits give ways to make claims about entire pieces of shape instead of guessing from individual samples. Energy terms, which are scores that rise when a surface bends, intersects, drifts, or carries stress badly, let several demands be balanced at once. Differential operators and harmonic maps describe how quantities change across a surface, so smoothing, curvature, uncertainty, and constant-curvature design can be handled as surface behavior rather than image cleanup. Fields are useful because they assign values throughout space or over a domain, which lets printing paths, skeleton confidence, fabric fibers, or generated signals be followed continuously instead of as disconnected decisions.
paper_family: The representative papers fit together because each protects a different relationship while changing or querying geometry. Texture-Aware Remeshing changes the triangle layout but moves texture information onto vertices so later geometry operations still see appearance. Iskra asks how existing geometry programs can run backward, so a desired output can tell the input shape how to change. The winding-number papers and the Hausdorff-distance papers make inside-out and surface-distance questions faster by replacing exhaustive checks with ray tests, boundary formulas, branch-and-bound, buffers, moments, and certified subdivision. Feature-Preserving Offset Meshing, the NURBS intersection algorithm, Structural MAT, and Subgrid Marching Tetrahedra all guard structural details while deriving new surfaces, intersections, skeleton-like medial descriptions, or fine sheets from imperfect discrete input. Untangling Surfaces and Stress-Aware Panelization score the shape against physical or geometric violations, then adjust it to remove crossings or balance stress and fidelity. Strips as Tokens, Matern Noise, AniGen, Tempo3D, ACT, and virtual try-on bring the same concern into learned generation: the output must carry connections, UV boundaries, skeletons, motion, or garment correspondences, not just look plausible. Cloth capture, fabric capture, kirigami, AtomSlicer, and MorphSkein show the same logic when shape must obey cameras, fibers, cuts, print beads, or pixel density.
what_changed: The 2026 pattern in this evidence is that geometry processing is less isolated from the rest of graphics. Classical questions such as distance, intersection, inside-out tests, remeshing, offsets, medial axes, and curvature are still present, but they are being pushed onto GPUs, made certified, or connected to uncertainty. At the same time, generated and captured shapes are expected to arrive with usable structure: UV boundaries, skeletons, skinning, garment correspondences, cloth motion, fabric fibers, and surface signals. Fabrication and display papers also demand geometry that respects physical constraints such as bead thickness, deployability, stress, collision freedom, and pixel density. The shift is from producing a surface to producing a surface that remains actionable.
limits: The evidence does not prove a single universal geometry method. Many results depend on assumptions about the input: triangle meshes, NURBS curves and patches, UV parameterization, clean or dirty surfaces, high-resolution meshes, microscopic images, bracketed exposures, planar graphs, or known garment and body proxies. Several approaches rely on discretization, floating-point arithmetic, learned models, or simulators, so their guarantees may weaken outside the tested setting. Speedups for winding numbers, Hausdorff distance, neural surface queries, or hair scattering do not automatically transfer to every model size, tolerance, hardware layout, or visual case. The abstracts also state contributions more than failures. They do not fully establish behavior on extreme self-intersections, missing texture evidence, unusual skeletons, severe capture occlusion, unsupported materials, or fabrication machines with different physical limits.
